I understand the Flash hate that's been going around for years now. I get that people don't like the closed nature of this proprietary platform. I know it has vulnerabilities galore. I agree with all of this. But, what I don't get is why Adobe (Macromedie) Flex had to be a victim in all of this too. Flex and its companion technology AIR (Adobe Integrated Runtime) was something I felt could unify the OS platforms the way Java had promised to do and failed to deliver on. I've built many desktop and mobile apps with AIR over the years. MXML, the markup language in Flex, is less of a mess than HTML and CSS. ActionScript doesn't suffer from many of the problems JavaScript does. I could write one codebase and deploy to Windows, MacOS, Android and iOS with ease. It was even made open source before Adobe axed it and is fully open now that Apache owns it. All of that is gone now save for some diehards like me.

Compared to building things in current web technologies with endless frameworks, polyfills and CSS hacks, Flex and AIR just had a more seamless approach to building rich desktop, web and mobile apps but still being highly extensible. I dreamed of a day that browsers would have such a thing built in to allow apps to be built with similar technology and to relegate HTML and CSS to pure content markup functionality. Flex was headed that way until Steve Jobs fired shots. I miss what could have been great...

I'm probably going to be unpopular with this belief, but I'll stick by my guns as a senior software builder who has seen more technology come and go than most people on the Internet today. One day will come when you reach my age and experience and will wonder why technology looks like it's going backwards instead of innovating and improving. I recommend you grow a nice grey beard by that time so you can tell the kids to get off your LA(w)N.
